Define the logical boundary between query identity, execution, cached result metadata, and physical cache storage.

## Scope

Introduce or refine contracts for:

- Logical query identity
- Normalized query fingerprint
- Cache lookup request
- Cache lookup result
- Cache write request
- Cached artifact metadata
- Cache storage location abstraction
- Result lifecycle state

## Deliverables

- Java interfaces/classes for cache boundary contracts
- Documentation showing how cache sits between Databricks and higher-level consumers
- Tests for deterministic identity/fingerprint behavior where applicable

## Acceptance criteria

- Cache identity is separated from physical storage details
- Higher layers do not need to know whether storage is local, S3, or future-compatible object storage
- Contracts are usable by SQL Gateway today and Semantic Layer later
- Existing cache behavior is not broken

## Non-goals

- No full cache rewrite
- No distributed cache protocol
- No production object-store migration
- No semantic cache planner

# Lane C: C1 — Define Skadi platform boundary model

Parent epic: #38

## Objective

Define the architectural boundaries between the major Skadi platform components before implementation expands beyond the SQL Gateway.

## Scope

Document the responsibilities and non-responsibilities of:

- SQL Gateway
- Query Execution Layer
- Cache Layer
- Semantic Contract Layer
- Semantic Planner / Rule Engine, future only
- UI Brick Runtime, future only
- AI Chat Buddy, future only
- Databricks / Mesh / Gold data
- Market Risk Brain / unstructured knowledge, future integration
- BCBS239 lineage database, future integration

## Deliverables

- Markdown architecture document under `ai/architecture/` or equivalent
- Boundary diagram using Mermaid
- Clear "owns / does not own" table per component
- Explicit future-extension seams

## Acceptance criteria

- The document makes clear that Lane C is about contracts and skeletons, not full semantic implementation
- SQL Gateway remains focused on protocol and query-serving concerns
- Semantic layer is described as a contract boundary, not yet a full planner
- Cache layer is positioned between Databricks and higher-level consumers
- Future UI/AI systems are shown as consumers of contracts, not implemented here

## Non-goals

- No implementation of semantic planning
- No UI runtime

# Skadi Platform: Lane C — Contracts, Skeletons, and Architectural Boundaries


## Goal


Lane C establishes the architectural contracts, skeleton modules, service boundaries, and documentation needed before Skadi evolves into a broader semantic/query/UI platform.

This lane intentionally avoids building the full semantic planner, AI assistant, dashboard runtime, or entitlement engine.

## Why this lane exists


Lane A and Lane B proved and hardened the Tableau SQL Endpoint path.

The next architectural risk is not "can we build features?" but "can we preserve clean boundaries before the platform expands?"

Lane C creates the contracts and seams needed for future work across:

- SQL Gateway
- Cache Layer
- Semantic Layer
- UI Brick / dashboard layer
- AI Chat Buddy
- Databricks / Mesh / Gold data
- Lineage and Market Risk Brain integrations

## Explicit non-goals


Lane C does NOT implement:

- A full semantic planner
- A full AI chatbot
- A dashboard runtime
- Drag/drop UI composition
- Full semantic rule execution
- Entitlement engine implementation
- Production-grade lineage integration

## Success criteria


- Clear boundary model documented
- Core contract packages/classes introduced
- Query contract and output-shape metadata skeletons exist
- Cache/execution/semantic boundary interfaces exist
- ADRs or DQRs capture the major decisions
- Tests validate contract serialization and boundary behavior
- Existing SQL Gateway tests continue to pass

## Candidate stories


- C1 — Define Skadi platform boundary model
- C2 — Introduce semantic contract skeletons
- C3 — Define query contract and output-shape metadata
- C4 — Define cache contract boundary
- C5 — Define service interfaces for semantic-aware execution
- C6 — Add architecture docs / ADRs for Lane C boundaries
- C7 — Add contract-focused tests
- C8 — Add dev-status and runbook updates for Lane C

# Tableau SQL Endpoint (PostgreSQL/MySQL Wire-Protocol) — Epic & Story Breakdown

> **Goal:** Make Tableau (and other JDBC/ODBC clients) connect to **Skadi as a SQL endpoint** using **PostgreSQL or MySQL-like wire protocol**, while Skadi transparently accelerates/caches queries against **Databricks SQL Warehouse (MXL)**.
>
> **Approach (opinionated):**
> - **POC lane:** implement **PostgreSQL wire protocol first** (broadest ecosystem, stable semantics, easy Tableau testing via native Postgres connector).
> - Keep a thin dialect/adapter layer so **MySQL** can be added later without rewriting the DBX execution/caching core.
>
> **Non-goals (POC):**
> - Full SQL engine semantics (joins/compute stay in Databricks).
> - Full Tableau connector packaging (.taco) and enterprise auth (OIDC) — those are production lane items.
> - Row-level security policy engine in Skadi (prefer delegation to Databricks for POC).

---

## EPIC: Tableau SQL Endpoint (PostgreSQL/MySQL Protocol)

### Outcomes
- Tableau Desktop can connect to Skadi using a standard SQL connector (Postgres preferred).
- Tableau can browse schema (or at minimum run Custom SQL) and render 2–3 representative dashboards.
- Skadi caches metadata + query results and demonstrates measurable speedup on warm cache.
- Clear path to production hardening: auth, observability, correctness, load tests, and packaging.

### High-level Architecture (POC)
Tableau / JDBC client
 - (PostgreSQL wire protocol)
 - Skadi SQL Gateway
- session/auth (POC: basic)
- SQL normalize + parameter binding
- metadata endpoints (catalog/schema/table/columns)
- query routing + cancellation
- cache keying + result caching
- (JDBC/HTTP)
- Databricks SQL Warehouse (MXL datasets)
### Definition of Done (Epic)
- ✅ End-to-end demo: Tableau → Skadi (PG) → Databricks → results
- ✅ Warm-cache run shows reduced warehouse load + improved latency
- ✅ Basic correctness: types, nulls, timestamps, decimal scale, row counts
- ✅ Minimal security: authentication + per-user session isolation
- ✅ Documentation: setup + known limitations + troubleshooting
title: EPIC: Tableau SQL Endpoint (PostgreSQL/MySQL Protocol)

# EPIC: Performance & Benchmarking

## 🎯 Objective

Design and implement a **comprehensive performance and benchmarking framework** for Skadi to:

- Quantify acceleration vs direct Databricks access
- Measure Arrow streaming efficiency
- Validate cache effectiveness (local + S3)
- Detect regressions early
- Provide architecture-review-ready evidence

This epic ensures Skadi performance is **measurable, defensible, and continuously validated**.

---

## 🧊 Background

Skadi’s value proposition depends on:

- Large result sets (10M+ rows)
- Repeated query patterns (Tableau, grid compute)
- T-2 refresh cycles
- Cache reuse
- Arrow columnar streaming

In MXL / MXR-style environments:

- 200M rows per day
- Frequent intraday refresh
- Tableau full-table scan behavior
- Thousands of compute consumers

Without rigorous benchmarking:

- Performance claims are anecdotal
- Regressions go unnoticed
- Architecture boards remain skeptical

This epic creates **objective performance proof**.

---

# 📦 Scope of This Epic

---

## 1️⃣ Baseline Benchmark Framework

Establish reproducible test harness.

Must support:

- Direct Databricks SQL (baseline)
- Skadi → DB (no cache)
- Skadi → cache_local
- Skadi → cache_s3
- JSON vs Arrow comparison

Metrics captured:

- Total latency
- Time to first byte
- Throughput (rows/sec)
- Memory usage
- CPU usage
- Network bytes transferred

Deliverable:

- Reproducible benchmark scripts
- Configurable dataset sizes
- Version-controlled benchmark definitions

---

## 2️⃣ Arrow Streaming Performance

Measure:

- RecordBatch size impact
- Serialization cost
- Streaming vs full materialization
- Client-side deserialization cost
- Pandas conversion time

Test scales:

- 1M rows
- 10M rows
- 50M rows (if feasible)
- Wide vs narrow schemas

Target outcomes:

- ≥ 3x improvement vs JSON
- Stable memory usage
- No OOM at 10M+ rows

---

## 3️⃣ Cache Performance Evaluation

Evaluate:

- Cold cache (first execution)
- Warm local cache
- Warm S3 cache
- Cache invalidation cost
- Cache rebuild time

Measure:

- Hit ratio
- Latency improvement
- Storage overhead
- Network egress cost
- Cache read throughput

Validate:

- Cache_local faster than DB
- Cache_s3 competitive at scale
- No corruption under concurrency

---

## 4️⃣ Concurrency & Load Testing

Simulate:

- 10 concurrent users
- 50 concurrent users
- 200+ concurrent grid consumers

Measure:

- Throughput scaling
- Thread pool behavior
- Connection pool saturation
- Memory growth
- GC pressure
- Latency distribution (P50, P95, P99)

Validate:

- No deadlocks
- No memory leaks
- Stable under sustained load

---

## 5️⃣ Query Pattern Benchmarking

Simulate realistic workloads:

- Full-table scans (Tableau)
- Group-by aggregation
- Filtered subset queries
- Repeated identical queries
- T-2 refresh invalidation scenario

Evaluate:

- Impact of weird Tableau-generated SQL
- Cache invalidation effectiveness
- Repeated access acceleration

---

## 6️⃣ Resource Profiling

Capture:

- JVM heap usage
- Off-heap Arrow memory usage
- CPU usage
- GC metrics
- Network utilization

Provide:

- Profiling reports
- Memory allocation breakdown
- Leak detection validation

---

## 7️⃣ Regression Benchmark Suite

Integrate into CI/CD:

- Run microbenchmarks on PR
- Run performance smoke tests
- Detect >10% regression automatically
- Fail build if threshold exceeded

Maintain:

- Historical benchmark trend data
- Version-to-version comparison
- Performance changelog

---

## 8️⃣ Cost Efficiency Analysis

For enterprise environments, measure:

- Compute savings
- DB load reduction
- Network egress reduction
- Cache storage cost vs compute savings

Produce:

- Example cost model
- Acceleration ROI analysis
- Architecture board-ready summary

---

## 9️⃣ Performance Documentation

Produce:

- Benchmark methodology document
- Reproducibility instructions
- Hardware configuration disclosure
- Environment specification
- Dataset generation scripts

Must ensure:

- Results are transparent
- Results are reproducible
- Results are credible

---

# 📊 Benchmark Dimensions

Test matrix must include:

| Dimension | Variants |
|-----------|----------|
| Transport | JSON / Arrow |
| Cache | None / Local / S3 |
| Concurrency | 1 / 10 / 50 / 200 |
| Dataset size | 1M / 10M / 50M |
| Schema width | Narrow / Wide |
| Query pattern | Scan / Filter / Group-by |

---

# 🔐 Non-Functional Requirements

- Reproducible
- Version-controlled
- Automated where possible
- Low operational overhead
- Safe for shared environments
- No interference with production

---

# 🚫 Out of Scope (Separate Epics)

- Advanced adaptive query planning
- Automatic cache prewarming
- Cluster autoscaling logic
- GPU acceleration
- Cross-region replication benchmarks

---

# 📈 Why This Matters

For MXL / MXR environments:

- Performance must be provable
- Cache value must be quantified
- Arrow benefits must be measurable
- Architecture boards require evidence
- Cost savings must be defensible

Without this epic:

- Skadi remains anecdotal
- Claims are not credible
- Enterprise adoption slows

With it:

- Skadi is defensible

- Regressions are caught early
- Enterprise confidence increases

Once complete, Skadi becomes:

# EPIC: Security & Auth

## 🎯 Objective

Design and implement **enterprise-grade security and authentication** for Skadi so it can be safely deployed in regulated environments (e.g., financial institutions running MXL / MXR workloads).

This epic establishes:

- Strong authentication
- Authorization controls
- Secure transport
- Secret handling best practices
- Auditability
- Production hardening

Skadi must not be a “dev-only proxy.” It must be a secure, review-board-ready data plane component.

---

## 🧊 Background

Skadi:

- Sits between clients (Python, Tableau, semantic layer) and Databricks
- Streams large Arrow result sets
- Caches potentially sensitive data (risk, PnL, positions)
- May operate in shared infrastructure
- May expose SQL execution capability

In market risk environments:

- Data is highly sensitive
- Regulatory scrutiny is real
- Access must be controlled
- Audit trails are required

Security must be foundational, not bolted on.

---

# 📦 Scope of This Epic

---

## 1️⃣ Authentication Layer

Implement pluggable authentication mechanisms.

### Phase 1 (Required)

- API Key authentication
- Bearer token authentication
- Configurable header name
- Secure comparison (constant-time check)
- Token hashing (no plaintext storage in logs)

### Phase 2 (Enterprise-ready)

- OAuth2 / OIDC integration
- JWT validation (issuer, audience, expiry)
- JWKS support
- Token signature verification
- Role claim extraction

### Requirements

- Authentication enforced on all non-health endpoints
- No anonymous query access
- Configurable auth enable/disable (dev mode only)
- Clear 401 vs 403 responses

---

## 2️⃣ Authorization Model

Implement basic role-based access control (RBAC).

### Role Examples

- `admin`
- `read`
- `query`
- `monitor`
- `cache_admin`

### Controls

- Restrict query execution
- Restrict monitoring access
- Restrict cache invalidation
- Restrict configuration endpoints

### Requirements

- Role extracted from token or config mapping
- Endpoint-level authorization rules
- Deny-by-default posture
- Clear audit logging of denied attempts

---

## 3️⃣ Transport Security

### TLS Support

- HTTPS support
- Configurable keystore
- TLS 1.2+
- Secure cipher defaults
- Certificate validation for outbound calls

### Mutual TLS (Future-capable)

- Client certificate support
- Truststore configuration
- Optional mTLS enforcement

### Requirements

- No plaintext credentials in transit
- Configurable redirect HTTP → HTTPS
- Production-ready TLS config documentation

---

## 4️⃣ Secure Secret Handling

Ensure:

- No secrets stored in code
- Environment variable support
- Externalized configuration (Spring config)
- Vault-compatible integration pattern
- Secure logging (no secret leakage)

Must support:

- API keys
- Databricks tokens
- S3 credentials
- Future IAM credentials

---

## 5️⃣ Query Security Controls

Mitigate risks of arbitrary SQL execution.

### Controls

- Optional query allowlist
- Optional schema restrictions
- Configurable max result size
- Configurable max execution time
- Rate limiting (basic)
- Payload size limits

### Protections

- Prevent resource exhaustion
- Prevent uncontrolled full-table scans (optional guardrails)
- Protect against denial-of-service

---

## 6️⃣ Cache Security

Because Skadi caches data:

- Encrypted S3 storage (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS)
- Local disk encryption compatibility
- Secure cache key design
- No raw SQL in cache path
- No PII leakage in cache metadata

Must ensure:

- Cache access respects authorization
- Cache invalidation requires proper role
- Cache entries not accessible cross-tenant (future)

---

## 7️⃣ Audit Logging

Implement structured audit logging.

Log:

- Auth attempts (success/failure)
- Query executions
- Cache hits/misses
- Cache invalidations
- Admin operations
- Configuration changes

Requirements:

- Structured JSON logs
- No secret exposure
- Correlation ID support
- Traceable query ID mapping

---

## 8️⃣ Observability & Security Metrics

Expose:

- Auth failure count
- Rate limit triggers
- Unauthorized access attempts
- Token validation errors
- TLS handshake failures

Via:

- Actuator metrics
- Monitoring API
- Logs

---

## 9️⃣ Hardening & Secure Defaults

Skadi must:

- Disable dev-only endpoints in prod
- Disable default credentials
- Disable unsecured modes by default
- Enforce authentication when profile = prod
- Validate configuration at startup

Fail fast if:

- Auth required but no auth configured
- TLS required but misconfigured
- Invalid JWT issuer

---

# 🔐 Non-Functional Requirements

- Thread-safe auth filters
- No significant latency overhead
- Clean separation of auth logic
- Pluggable auth provider architecture
- Production-ready error handling
- Secure default config templates
- Compatible with enterprise security review

---

# 🚫 Out of Scope (Separate Epics)

- Full multi-tenant isolation
- Fine-grained row-level security
- Data masking engine
- External IAM policy engine
- Advanced WAF integration
- Security compliance automation

---

# 📊 Why This Matters

For MXL / MXR environments:

- Risk data is sensitive

# EPIC: UI & Monitoring Dashboard

## 🎯 Objective

Design and implement a **production-grade UI & Monitoring Dashboard** for Skadi that provides:

- Real-time visibility into query performance
- Clear separation of cached vs non-cached queries
- Cache effectiveness metrics
- Streaming performance visibility (Arrow)
- Operational observability for enterprise environments

The dashboard must feel **serious, enterprise-grade, and Databricks-aligned**, not experimental.

---

## 🧊 Background

Skadi is evolving into:

- A columnar streaming data plane
- A distributed cache layer (local + S3)
- A query acceleration engine for Databricks SQL
- A foundation for MXL / MXR-scale workloads

With:

- 200M rows per day
- T-2 refresh every 2 hours
- Tableau full-table scan patterns
- Grid compute workloads

We require a UI that:

- Clearly demonstrates acceleration value
- Surfaces cache hit behavior
- Enables operational debugging
- Supports performance benchmarking

---

## 🏗 Target UX Principles

Inspired by Databricks SQL Warehouse monitoring:

- White background
- Clean enterprise layout
- Time-series graph at top
- History grid at bottom
- Minimal noise
- Precise metrics
- Small, readable timestamps
- No diagonal axis text
- Git-style short IDs (last 6 chars)

---

## 📊 Dashboard Layout

### Top Section: Time-Series Performance Graph

Display:

- Query duration over time
- Two lines:
  - Cached queries (green or blue)
  - Non-cached queries (gray or orange)
- Horizontal time labels (small font, not rotated)
- Hover tooltips showing:
  - Full query ID
  - Duration
  - Cache type
  - Row count
  - Timestamp

Metrics shown:

- P50
- P95
- Average duration
- Cache hit ratio

---

### Bottom Section: Query History Grid

Columns:

- Timestamp
- Query ID (last 6 chars, hover shows full ID)
- Abbreviated SQL (ellipsis with hover full text)
- Duration (ms)
- Row count
- Cache source:
  - `cache_local`
  - `cache_s3`
  - `db`
- Mode (interactive / batch)

Requirements:

- Accurate row count (must not default to 0)
- Real cache type values
- Sortable columns
- Filter by:
  - Cache type
  - Date range
  - Mode
- Pagination or infinite scroll

---

## 📦 Scope of This Epic

---

## 1️⃣ Query History Backend API

Create endpoint: GET /api/monitoring/metrics


Provides:

- Time-series data (bucketed)
- Cache hit ratio
- P50 / P95 latency
- Total queries
- Arrow streaming duration metrics
- DB execution vs cache retrieval time

Must be efficient and non-blocking.

---

## 3️⃣ Real-Time Updates

Support:

- Polling refresh (default)
- Optional WebSocket support (future)
- Auto-refresh interval (configurable)

Must not:

- Interfere with query execution
- Add significant overhead

---

## 4️⃣ Graph Implementation

Requirements:

- Smooth rendering for 1000+ datapoints
- Distinct color lines
- Tooltip precision
- No rotated time labels
- Clean spacing
- Lightweight charting library

Must handle:

- Large time ranges
- Sparse intervals
- High-volume bursts

---

## 5️⃣ Cache Visibility

Clearly show:

- Local cache hits
- S3 cache hits
- DB fallback

Display:

- Hit ratio percentage
- Volume of data served from cache
- Estimated time saved

---

## 6️⃣ Streaming Observability

Expose:

- Rows streamed
- Batches streamed
- Stream duration
- Bytes transferred
- Client disconnects
- Partial stream failures

Visible in:

- Query detail modal
- Metrics API

---

## 7️⃣ Query Detail Modal

On row click:

Show:

- Full SQL
- Full query ID
- Execution breakdown:
  - Planning time
  - DB execution time
  - Cache retrieval time
  - Arrow serialization time
  - Stream duration
- Cache key
- Memory usage
- Error message (if applicable)

---

## 8️⃣ Error Visibility

Clearly surface:

- Failed queries
- Timeout errors
- Stream interruptions
- Cache invalidations

Errors must be:

- Visible
- Searchable
- Traceable

---

## 9️⃣ Performance & Scalability

Dashboard must:

- Handle 100K+ history records
- Avoid loading entire dataset in memory
- Use paginated backend queries
- Remain responsive under load

---

## 🔐 Non-Functional Requirements

- Secure endpoints (auth protected)
- No sensitive SQL leakage without permission
- Enterprise-grade UI polish
- Responsive layout
- Clean CSS
- Production-ready build process
- Thread-safe metrics collection
- Low runtime overhead

---

## 🚫 Out of Scope (Separate Epics)

- Multi-tenant view isolation
- Role-based UI filtering
- Advanced alerting system
- SLA breach notifications
- Cluster autoscaling dashboard
- Cost tracking analytics

---

## 📈 Why This Matters

For MXL / MXR-scale systems:

- Architects need proof of acceleration
- Ops teams need observability
- Developers need debugging visibility
- Risk compute needs performance guarantees

Without a serious dashboard:

- Skadi looks like a proxy

- Acceleration is unprovable

With it:

- Operational maturity is clear
- Enterprise adoption is easier

- [ ] Performance benchmarks documented
- [ ] Documentation updated

- Observable
- Measurable
- Enterprise-ready

# EPIC: Python Client (skadi-python-client)

## 🎯 Objective

Design and deliver a **production-grade Python client library** for Skadi that enables:

- High-performance Arrow streaming consumption
- Seamless integration with Pandas / PyArrow / NumPy
- Efficient distributed compute usage (risk grids, analytics clusters)
- Clean developer ergonomics
- Secure and observable API interaction

The Python client is the **primary consumption interface** for grid compute and analytics workloads.

---

## 🧊 Background

Skadi’s core transport layer is based on:

- Apache Arrow streaming
- Columnar result delivery
- Local + S3 cache acceleration
- Databricks SQL integration

To unlock Skadi’s value for:

- Market risk grid compute
- Large batch VaR / Greeks runs
- Distributed scenario engines
- Research notebooks
- ML pipelines

We require a robust Python client that:

- Streams Arrow efficiently
- Avoids unnecessary memory duplication
- Supports iterative batch processing
- Works at scale (10M+ rows)

---

## 🏗 Target Architecture
Python Client
↓
HTTP POST /api/query
↓
Arrow Stream (chunked)
↓
pyarrow.ipc.open_stream()
↓
Batch iterator or full table materialization

Deliverable:

- Pip-installable package
- PEP-compliant packaging
- Clean public API surface
- Versioned releases

---

## 2️⃣ Core API Design

Primary interface:

```python
from skadi import SkadiClient

client = SkadiClient(
    base_url="http://skadi-host:8090",
    api_key="...",
    timeout=300
)

df = client.query(
    sql="SELECT * FROM mxl_gold.var",
    as_of="2025-03-31",
    mode="interactive"
)
```

SQL-based query

Semantic query mode (future compatible)

Arrow streaming mode (default)

JSON fallback mode (optional)

3️⃣ Arrow Streaming Support

Must support:

HTTP chunked Arrow stream

pyarrow.ipc.open_stream

Iterative record batch consumption

Optional full-table materialization

Two consumption modes:

A) Full materialization
df = client.query(...).to_pandas()

B) Streaming iterator
for batch in client.stream(...):
    process(batch)
Requirements:

No full buffering in memory

Efficient conversion to Pandas

Preserve Arrow schema fidelity

Decimal and timestamp precision maintained

4️⃣ Distributed Compute Optimization

Client must:

Avoid redundant copies

Support multiprocessing

Be safe under concurrent execution

Reuse HTTP sessions

Handle retry logic gracefully

Target environments:

Python risk grids

Airflow DAGs

Databricks notebooks

Jupyter research

Batch scenario engines

5️⃣ Authentication & Security

Support:

API key header

Bearer token

Future IAM-based integration

Features:

Secure header injection

Timeout control

TLS verification

Configurable retry policy

6️⃣ Error Handling

Define custom exceptions:

SkadiConnectionError

SkadiTimeoutError

SkadiQueryError

SkadiStreamError

SkadiAuthError

Must:

Surface meaningful server error messages

Detect partial stream failure

Handle client disconnect cleanly

7️⃣ Performance Validation

Benchmark:

Arrow streaming vs JSON

Batch size tuning

Memory footprint

Throughput (rows/sec)

Target:

≥ 3x faster than JSON consumption

Minimal peak memory overhead

Stable under 10M+ row streams

8️⃣ Observability & Telemetry

Expose:

Query duration

Bytes received

Rows processed

Batch count

Retry attempts

Optional:

Logging integration

Metrics hooks

OpenTelemetry compatibility (future)

9️⃣ Testing Strategy

Include:

Unit tests (pytest)

Integration tests against local Skadi

Mock streaming tests

Large stream simulation tests

Decimal precision validation tests

Timestamp timezone tests

Target coverage:

≥ 80%

🔐 Non-Functional Requirements

Thread-safe

Memory-safe

Python 3.9+

Clean dependency tree

No unnecessary heavy dependencies

Deterministic cleanup of stream resources

🚫 Out of Scope (Separate Epics)

Async client (future epic)

gRPC / Arrow Flight client

Pandas extension types

Native C acceleration

Dask integration

The bridge between Skadi and compute

# EPIC: Arrow Streaming API

## 🎯 Objective

Design and implement a **production-grade Apache Arrow streaming API** for Skadi that enables high-performance, low-latency, columnar result delivery to downstream clients (Python grids, analytics engines, Tableau connectors, semantic layers, etc.).

This epic establishes Arrow streaming as the **primary data transport protocol** for Skadi.

---

## 🧊 Background

Skadi’s core value proposition is:

- Accelerate large SQL result sets from Databricks
- Avoid repeated full scans of large Delta tables
- Provide distributed caching (local + S3)
- Deliver results efficiently to thousands of compute nodes

Traditional JSON/CSV transport is:

- Row-based
- CPU heavy
- Serialization inefficient
- Not zero-copy
- Poor for large datasets (e.g., 200M rows/day in PIT gold tables)

**Apache Arrow streaming** enables:

- Columnar transport
- Zero-copy deserialization
- SIMD/vectorized processing
- Native Pandas/NumPy compatibility
- Efficient memory reuse
- Binary compactness

---

## 🏗 Target Architecture
HTTP POST /api/query
↓
Skadi Execution Layer
↓
Databricks SQL Warehouse
↓
ResultSet → Arrow RecordBatch Stream
↓
Arrow IPC Streaming (chunked transfer)
↓
Client Arrow Reader


---

## 📦 Scope of This Epic

### 1️⃣ Core Arrow Streaming Endpoint

- Content-Type: `application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream`
- Chunked HTTP transfer encoding
- RecordBatch streaming
- Backpressure-safe
- Zero full materialization in memory

Deliverable:
- `/api/query` supports Arrow streaming mode
- Optional `Accept` header negotiation

---

### 2️⃣ ResultSet → Arrow Conversion Layer

- Convert JDBC ResultSet to Arrow VectorSchemaRoot
- Type mapping:
  - Decimal → Arrow Decimal128
  - Timestamp → Arrow Timestamp (with timezone)
  - String → VarCharVector
  - Boolean → BitVector
- Configurable batch size
- Memory pool management
- Explicit vector lifecycle handling

Deliverable:
- Reusable ArrowWriter utility
- Deterministic memory cleanup
- No memory leaks under load

---

### 3️⃣ Streaming Semantics

Support:

- RecordBatch streaming (not full-table buffering)
- Large dataset handling (10M+ rows)
- Early client consumption
- Stream termination on error
- Proper Arrow footer handling

Must ensure:

- Client can read progressively
- Stream integrity preserved
- Partial batches handled safely

---

### 4️⃣ Python Client Compatibility

Skadi Python client must:

- Accept Arrow streaming response
- Use `pyarrow.ipc.open_stream`
- Convert to Pandas efficiently
- Support:
  - Full materialization
  - Iterative batch processing

Deliverable:
- Example client usage
- Integration test
- End-to-end validation

---

### 5️⃣ Performance Validation

Benchmark against:

- JSON response
- CSV response
- Non-streamed Arrow file

Metrics:

- Throughput (rows/sec)
- Memory usage
- CPU usage
- Latency to first byte
- Total transfer time

Target:

- ≥ 3x throughput vs JSON
- ≤ 50% memory footprint vs materialized JSON
- Near-linear scalability with batch size tuning

---

### 6️⃣ Observability & Metrics

Expose via Spring Boot Actuator:

- Rows streamed
- Batches streamed
- Stream duration
- Errors
- Memory pool utilization

History UI must reflect:

- Arrow streaming duration
- Cache hit type (cache_local / cache_s3 / db)

---

### 7️⃣ Failure Modes

Handle:

- Client disconnect mid-stream
- JDBC timeout
- Arrow serialization failure
- Memory exhaustion
- Partial batch write

Must:

- Close vectors
- Close allocator
- Release JDBC resources
- Not corrupt connection pool

---

## 🚫 Out of Scope (Separate Epics)

- Arrow Flight protocol
- gRPC transport
- Peer-to-peer Arrow replication
- Compressed stream optimization
- TLS mutual auth enhancements
- Semantic layer aggregation engine

---

## 🧪 Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `/api/query` returns valid Arrow stream
- [ ] Python client successfully consumes stream
- [ ] 10M+ rows streamed without OOM
- [ ] No memory leaks under load test
- [ ] Backpressure-safe
- [ ] Benchmark shows measurable performance improvement
- [ ] All tests passing (unit + integration)
- [ ] Documentation updated
- [ ] Example notebook provided

---

## 🔐 Non-Functional Requirements

- Thread-safe
- Production-grade error handling
- Graceful shutdown safe
- No full materialization for large result sets
- Secure header validation
- Compatible with Skadi cache layer

---

## 📚 Technical Dependencies

- Apache Arrow Java
- Apache Arrow Memory allocator
- Spring Boot streaming support
- Databricks JDBC driver
- Skadi cache abstraction

---

## 📊 Why This Matters

For MXL/MXR-scale risk data:

- 200M rows per day
- Frequent T-2 refresh
- Tableau weird full scans
- Thousands of grid nodes

Arrow streaming is:

- The foundation for Skadi as a **high-performance data plane**
- The enabler for distributed compute acceleration
- The backbone for future Arrow Flight support
- Critical for semantic layer (Runa) integration

---

## 🔥 Strategic Outcome

Once complete, Skadi becomes:

- A columnar streaming engine
- Not just a cache
- Not just a proxy
- But a data transport layer optimized for modern analytics

---

## 🧊 Related Epics

- EPIC: Skadi Local + S3 Cache Layer
- EPIC: Query Planner & Cache Invalidation
- EPIC: Semantic Layer Integration (Runa)
- EPIC: Arrow Flight Support

---
